Inter-assessor agreement

This assessment is DUAL — two assessors from different model families, the second asked blind. The agreement rate is withheld pending adjudication. Both readers were given this review’s decision rule; an earlier version of this sentence said the blinding had withheld it, and that was wrong. What the 10 domain comparison(s) show is a reading difference that runs in OPPOSITE directions by domain — on domains 1 to 3 the second assessor more often declines to judge at all, and on domains 4 and 5 it more often judges low. A single agreement rate averages those two behaviours into one number that describes neither. Both assessors’ per-result judgements are shown in the table above, unadjudicated, and neither is this review’s finding. No adjudication has been performed, so this review holds no final risk-of-bias judgement for these results.

Does the answer depend on the pooling method?

With two or three studies the Cochrane Handbook (10.10.4.4–10.10.4.5) asks for a sensitivity analysis comparing interval methods rather than a choice between them. Both are given here; the published interval is the first row.

Table 6. Does the answer depend on the pooling method?
IntervalMethodSummary (95% CI)
as publishedREML0.2606 (0.1766 to 0.3845)
sensitivity (Handbook 10.10.4.5)REML with Hartung-Knapp, t on k-1 = 1 degree(s) of freedom (t = 12.7062)0.2606 (0.0209 to 3.2461)

The published point is 0.2605 and the house-rule point is 0.2606. The number a reader remembers does not move; what differs is the precision claim. That is why nothing downstream catches this -- every memorable quantity survives.

A floor of 1 is applied to the variance-inflation factor so the adjustment can never narrow an interval below the unadjusted one. That guard is the recognised modification for exactly this instability, and its existence is evidence the small-k behaviour is a known problem with known handling rather than a novel judgement.

Why this is not an adjudicated disputeA blind second assessor from a different model family disagreed with this domain on 89% of judgements across 22 topics. How this maps to the tool s algorithmThe tool maps 'No information' on 1.1 and 1.2 with no baseline concern to a domain judgement of some concerns. This project writes no information on the domain when it could not be judged from the sources read, and caps the overall at some concerns. It does not replace the stored `judgement` beside it, and nothing reads it yet. The tool itself says its algorithms "provide proposed judgements, but users should verify these and change them if they feel this is appropriate" -- so this is an input to a person, not an output to a reader.
And it bounds a finding of oursClass 94 records assessor 2 saying no information on the randomisation process/deviations from the intended intervention/missing outcome data `100 of 100`. Measured across all 23 topics now stored that is 239 of 243, and all four exceptions are the randomisation process=some concerns on `agyw-hiv-prep-review` and `cab-prep-hiv-review` -- two of the three topics asked under the earlier prompt build, the one whose reply ids are bare NCTs. Under that build it is 4 of 6; under the later build 0 of 75. The 100% was measured on the later build's topics. The two-defaults mechanism stands; its universality does not, and what varies with it is the prompt.
The rate is still conditional on the same allow listBoth numbers are conditional on the fact list in THE_ALLOW_LIST_THE_RATE_IS_CONDITIONAL_ON above. Neither is a rate of agreement between assessors in general.
The finding of this comparisonA coverage finding, not an estimand one. Lien et al. 2026 included SIX randomised trials totalling 12,086 participants; This object pools two, totalling 4,465 as registered. Which six is not established -- the abstract names none and no included-study table was read -- so the four this object does not carry are counted and not identified. This is not a class-76 instance: they did not choose a better-defined target, they pooled more of the same kind. Whether this review's search should be widened is a content decision.

Introduction

Background. This review asks: In Nirsevimab versus placebo for medically attended RSV lower respiratory tract infection in infants, what is the effect on versus placebo on medically attended RSV lower respiratory tract infection? It pools 2 randomised trials, against placebo. The outcome pooled is medically attended RSV lower respiratory tract infection. Every count and denominator behind those estimates is read as follows. Registry throughout. Counts and denominators read from ClinicalTrials.gov posted results.1

Sources for this section (1)
  1. manuscript.introduction

Methods — search

Primary trials. No bibliographic search for primary trials was run. The 2 included trials were identified by reading named registrations on 2026-08-18. All three seeded registrations read on 2026-08-18 including arm types and posted results. Published syntheses. PubMed E-utilities esearch + esummary, executed 2026-08-21. Query as executed: (nirsevimab[tiab] OR MEDI8897[tiab]) and (meta-analysis[pt] OR "systematic review"[pt] OR meta-analysis[tiab] OR "pooled"[tiab] or melody[tiab]). It matched 39 record(s), of which 39 were retrieved and 39 read; 1 appraised.1

Methods — synthesis

For medically attended RSV lower respiratory tract infection, a random-effects model was fitted with the REML estimator.1

Risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2 (Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomized trials) , following . 2 result-level assessments were made.2

A ceiling applies to every risk-of-bias judgement in this review; it is stated with the assessment itself rather than summarised here.3

Certainty of evidence was rated with GRADE, following the Cochrane Handbook chapter 14. Randomised evidence starts HIGH and is rated down with reasons., following . 1 pooled outcome(s) were rated. No domain is rated UP. Rating up applies to observational evidence; these are randomised trials starting HIGH.4

Results

The pooled risk ratio for medically attended RSV lower respiratory tract infection was 0.261 (0.177 to 0.385) across 2 trials, against placebo.1

Noted on this pool. A published systematic review of this agent included six randomised trials (n = 12,086) where this pool carries two. Lien et al., Pediatrics and Neonatology 2026, PMID 41314935, reports RSV-related hospitalisation at OR 0.19 (0.13 to 0.30) and severe RSV infection at OR 0.23 (0.12 to 0.44). Those are different outcomes on a different scale from this pool's medically attended RSV lrti risk ratio of 0.2605 (0.1766 to 0.3845), so no discrepancy is claimed -- the point is the trial count. A published synthesis of this question included 6 trials where this pool carries 2. Source: Lien et al., Pediatrics and Neonatology 2026, PMID 41314935, six randomised trials totalling 12,086 participants. Which trials are absent is not established. The published abstract names none of its included studies and no included-study table was read, so this is a difference in stated counts and nothing more. It is not a claim that 4 specific trials were missed, and nobody here has identified them. The review's abstract names none of its six trials and no included-study table was read, so the four trials this object does not carry are counted and not identified. Naming them would require reading the review. The estimate above is computed from the trials this object carries and is not withdrawn or altered by this note. What a reader is owed is the scope: a larger evidence base on this question exists in the literature, and whether this review's search should be widened is a decision that has not been made.2

The trials' results were closely consistent with one another: I-squared, the share of the variation between them that is more than chance alone would produce, was 0%; the estimated variance of the true effects between trials (tau-squared) was 0, the heterogeneity test statistic Q was 0.0876, on degrees of freedom 1.3

What this does not establish: Not that either trial is free of bias -- no risk-of-bias assessment is recorded. Not anything about the excluded open-label trial, which reports a large effect on its own terms and is excluded on comparator type, not on quality. Not RSV hospitalisation or mortality, neither of which is the pooled endpoint. Not reliability at k=2 -- see Hartung-Knapp.4

The full model output for every pooled outcome -- the call, the estimator, the heterogeneity statistics and the back-transformed interval -- is stored verbatim on this review object at `results.by_outcome.<outcome>.r_output.verbatim`. It is not reproduced as an Extended data section in this article; an earlier version of this sentence said it was, and no such section exists.5

Risk of bias in the included results

Risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2 at the level of each reported result, by two assessors reading independently. Their judgements differ on 2 of the 2 results and no adjudication has been performed, so this review holds no final risk-of-bias judgement for these results. Assessor 1 recorded: 2 at some concerns. Assessor 2 recorded: 2 at no information. Both are shown in the risk-of-bias table; neither is the review's finding. The per-domain judgements behind them are recorded with the extracted data.1

Certainty of the evidence

Certainty was rated with GRADE, following the Cochrane Handbook chapter 14. Randomised evidence starts HIGH and is rated down with reasons..1

No domain is rated UP. Rating up applies to observational evidence; these are randomised trials starting HIGH.2

This certainty rating is pending, not rated. It rests on a risk-of-bias judgement that this review has not finalised: two assessors read every contributing result independently, they disagree, and no adjudication has been performed, so this review holds no final risk-of-bias judgement for these results. Cochrane rates certainty per outcome by aggregating the risk-of-bias judgements of the results contributing to it, so a certainty rating cannot be more final than the risk-of-bias assessment it reads. The rating this object currently records, and the steps behind it, are shown below as the work so far rather than as this review's answer. No level is published for this outcome -- not the recorded one, not a more cautious one, and not a midpoint -- because choosing one would be the judgement that has not been made.3

MODERATE certainty. The single downgrade is for two unjudgeable risk-of-bias domains that the registry does not carry -- not for inconsistency, indirectness or imprecision, none of which the evidence supports downgrading.4

Certainty of the evidence, by outcome, with every rating step5
OutcomeCertaintykStarted atRating steps
medically attended RSV lower respiratory tract infectionPending2HIGHthe steps taken so far, not a final rating: risk of bias -- Both results are some concerns, and the driver is not an observed weakness -- the randomisation process, measurement of the outcome and selection of the reported result are LOW on read registrations, with quadruple masking including the outcomes assessor. deviations from the intended intervention and missing outcome data are no information because the registry does not carry those fields, and an unjudgeable domain caps the overall. (move: HIGH to MODERATE, down 1 level(s)); inconsistency -- The stored refit gives tau^2 exactly zero, Q 0.0879 on 1 df, p = 0.7668; the two intervals -- 0.2715 (0.1689 to 0.4363) and 0.2395 (0.1214 to 0.4727) -- overlap almost entirely and agree in conclusion. (move: no downgrade); indirectness -- One registered primary on each trial, the same endpoint, placebo-controlled, and it is exactly what is pooled. Recorded and not used to downgrade: the two trials enrol different infant populations and NCT02878330 fixes a 50 mg dose where melody uses weight-banded dosing -- read from the registered arm labels. The endpoint definition is unaffected. (move: no downgrade); imprecision -- The effect is large and the interval excludes no difference by a wide margin: 0.2605 (0.1766 to 0.3845). Even the Hartung-Knapp interval at k = 2, 0.2606 (0.1233 to 0.5505) on t = 12.7062 with 1 df, excludes 1 across its whole range. Downgrading for imprecision here would be mechanical rather than warranted. (move: no downgrade); publication bias -- k = 2. Funnel-plot asymmetry tests have essentially no power below about ten trials (Handbook 13.3.5.4), so this is not assessable rather than 'undetected'. (move: Not assessable -- no rating applied)

Limitations

What this review does not give a clinician: the number of events in each arm, any absolute effect or number needed to treat and any measure of harm. A relative effect cannot be turned into the benefit or the risk facing one patient without them, so this review can support a judgement about what these trials found and not a judgement about what to do.1
